argument: In The Order of Things, Foucault studies not individual scientific discoveries but the unconscious background assumptions, which he calls 'epistemes,' that make a given era's science possible at all. Unlike Kuhn's paradigms, epistemes are unconscious and shape all the sciences of an era simultaneously, and they are maintained less through outright force than through 'normalizing power,' which gets people to feel that conforming is simply who they are, inverting Kant's project by showing that what seems necessarily true is actually historically contingent.
keyIdeas: Foucault studies the dichotomy between discursive formations (the language used to talk about institutions) and non-discursive formations (the institutions themselves, like hospitals and schools).

An episteme differs from Kuhn's paradigm: a paradigm is a consciously used set of best practices affecting one field, while an episteme is an unconscious set of assumptions shaping all the sciences of an era simultaneously, as shown by how the 18th versus 19th century description of a sick patient reflects a different background episteme.
The Renaissance episteme organized knowledge around resemblances between things, while the 18th-century episteme organized it around differences and taxonomy.
Normalizing power, unlike repressive power, works by getting people to feel that avoiding certain behavior is simply part of who they are, not something imposed by force.
Foucault inverts Kant's project: instead of analyzing the subjective to reach necessary truths, Foucault shows that things assumed to be necessary are actually subjective and rooted in history.

terms.def: The historical but unconscious background assumptions that ground knowledge and make it possible within a particular era.
The language used to talk about institutions versus the institutions (hospitals, schools, prisons) themselves.
The dominant, consciously used theories and practices of a scientific field at a given time, contrasted with Foucault's episteme.
Power that works by making people feel a behavior is part of their own identity, rather than compelling them by force.
The idea, popular in Foucault's era, that every science might eventually be reduced to physics.
